definition: A layered midbrain structure that maps visual, auditory and touch space and drives orienting movements of the eyes and head, such as saccades.
The cortical area that most directly drives voluntary movement, in front of the central sulcus. Its layer 5 neurons project down to the spinal cord.
An output nucleus of the basal ganglia. Its GABAergic neurons fire tonically and inhibit the thalamus and superior colliculus until the direct pathway pauses them.
A swelling on an axon, at its end or along it, that releases neurotransmitter at a synapse.
A cortical interneuron whose axon forms a tight vertical bundle (a horsetail) that inhibits the dendrites of cells in the same minicolumn.
A large cholinergic interneuron of the striatum that fires steadily and pauses when a reward or cue appears.

Dopamine acts through two families of receptors: D1-like receptors, which tend to excite and favour potentiation (direct-pathway striatal neurons), and D2-like receptors, which tend to inhibit (indirect-pathway neurons).
The membrane's ability to store charge, like a capacitor, about 1 µF per cm². With membrane resistance it sets how fast the voltage responds to current (the membrane time constant).
How much a neuron's voltage changes for a given injected current. Small neurons and closed channels mean high input resistance.
An ion channel that lets potassium ions out of the cell, pulling the voltage back down. The delayed rectifier ends the action potential; other types (A-type, M-type, SK) shape firing.
Inhibition whose reversal potential is near rest, so it barely changes the voltage but opens a leak that divides away excitatory input arriving nearby.
A connection from a higher to a lower stage of a hierarchy, carrying context, expectation or attention; in cortex it often targets layer 1 and the apical dendrites.
Responding strongly to some stimuli and weakly to others, e.g. a V1 neuron preferring one edge orientation.
Two ways a neuron can respond to input: an integrator adds inputs up and fires once enough arrive; a resonator fires best to inputs at its preferred frequency.
How strongly a neuron's output changes for a change in input; the slope of its input-output curve.
A closed loop in state space that a system goes around repeatedly; in a neuron model it is repetitive firing.
Hodgkin's classes of how neurons start firing: type I can fire at any low rate (integrators, often a saddle-node bifurcation); type II jumps to a minimum rate (resonators, often a Hopf bifurcation).
A commercial numerical computing environment and language, common in neuroscience labs.
Complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor, the transistor technology used for almost all modern chips.
A single chip that holds a whole computer: processors, memory controllers and interfaces.
The lowest-value bit of a binary number.
Hertz (Hz) counts cycles per second; a megahertz is a million per second. Firing rates are given in Hz, clock speeds in MHz or GHz.
A circuit that measures a voltage and turns it into a digital number.
The number of pixels a display shows, width by height, e.g. 640 × 480 for standard VGA.

term: Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers
definition: A professional association for engineering that publishes many journals and runs conferences, including several on neural networks and circuits.
An image format that describes drawings as shapes and lines, so they stay sharp at any size.
Retinal and thalamic cells that respond to light increments (ON cells) or decrements (OFF cells) in the centre of their receptive field. ON-OFF cells respond to both.
The family of neuron models that sum input in their membrane potential and fire a spike when it crosses a threshold, then reset, such as the LIF model.
A constant current, as opposed to an alternating or fluctuating one; in simulations, a steady input injected into neurons.
Machine Intelligence from Cortical Networks: a project that imaged the activity of a cubic millimetre of mouse visual cortex and then mapped its wiring with electron microscopy.
In the insect antennal lobe, an interneuron that connects glomeruli locally; also in this library, LN can mean the linear-nonlinear model.
A unit of memory size: about a million bytes (a byte is 8 bits). kB is a thousand bytes, GB a billion; kbit and Mbit count bits.
Razavi's picture of the eight mutually trading specifications of an analog circuit: gain, bandwidth, power, supply voltage, linearity, noise, swing and impedance.
Metal-oxide-semiconductor field-effect transistor: a voltage-controlled device whose gate voltage forms a conducting channel between source and drain.
The gate-source voltage ($V_{TH}$) at which a MOS transistor's channel begins to form and appreciable current flows.
$V_{GS}$ minus $V_{TH}$: how far the gate is above threshold. It sets the drain current, the transconductance and the minimum $V_{DS}$ needed for saturation.
The small-signal ratio of output current change to input voltage change; for a MOSFET $g_m = \frac{dI_D}{dV_{GS}} = \frac{2I_D}{V_{ov}}$ in saturation.
The region ($V_{DS} < V_{ov}$) where a MOSFET behaves like a voltage-controlled resistor.
The region ($V_{DS} \ge V_{ov}$) where a MOSFET's channel is pinched off and the drain current is nearly independent of $V_{DS}$; the normal operating region of analog amplifiers.
The rise in a MOSFET's threshold voltage when its source is at a higher voltage than its bulk ($V_{SB} > 0$).
The shortening of the effective channel as $V_{DS}$ rises in saturation, which makes drain current grow slightly with $V_{DS}$ and gives the transistor a finite output resistance.
The exponentially small drain current that flows below threshold; also called weak inversion. It offers the highest $g_m$ per unit current.
The product $g_m r_o$ of a transistor: the largest voltage gain obtainable from one device, equal to $\frac{2}{\lambda V_{ov}}$.
The small-signal resistance seen looking into a transistor's drain; $r_o = \frac{1}{\lambda I_D}$ in saturation.
The frequency at which a transistor's small-signal current gain drops to unity: $f_T = \frac{g_m}{2\pi(C_{gs} + C_{gd})}$.
The apparent multiplication of a capacitance bridging the input and output of an inverting amplifier by (1 + gain) as seen from the input.
The basic MOS voltage amplifier: input at the gate, output at the drain, source at the AC ground. Small-signal gain is $-g_m (R_D \parallel r_o)$.
A resistance in series with the source that trades gain for linearity: transconductance becomes $\frac{g_m}{1 + g_m R_S}$.
A transistor with gate shorted to drain, which behaves like a nonlinear resistance of about $1/g_m$.
A common-drain amplifier with gain just below one, high input impedance and low output impedance ($1/g_m$); used as a voltage buffer and level shifter.
An amplifier with signal at the source and output at the drain; low input resistance (about $1/g_m$), non-inverting.
A stack of a common-gate transistor on a common-source transistor that raises output resistance to about $g_m r_o^2$ and gain to about $(g_m r_o)^2$, at the cost of headroom.
A cascode whose upper device has the opposite polarity, so the signal current is folded to the other supply rail, saving voltage headroom.
A simplification for symmetric differential circuits: analyse one side with the symmetry axis treated as AC ground.
The ratio of a differential amplifier's differential gain to its common-mode-to-differential gain; a measure of how well it rejects common-mode interference.
How a differential circuit reacts to a signal applied equally to both inputs.
A multiplier made from stacked differential pairs whose output current is proportional to the product of two differential inputs; used as a mixer.
A circuit that copies a reference current to another branch by sharing the gate-source voltage of matched transistors.
An amplifier whose output is a current proportional to the differential input voltage; the five-transistor OTA is the simplest CMOS example.
A transistor used as a load, often a current mirror, giving high small-signal resistance with a small voltage drop.
Setting a transistor's DC operating point, usually via a current mirror from a stable reference.
The pole closest to the origin, which determines the bandwidth of an amplifier or the speed of a feedback system's response.
For a one-pole amplifier, the product of low-frequency gain and -3 dB bandwidth; it equals the unity-gain frequency.
Random voltage or current noise from the thermal motion of charge carriers; white, with PSD 4kTR for a resistor.
Low-frequency noise whose power density rises as 1/f, caused by traps at the gate-oxide interface; falls with larger device area.
The total thermal noise voltage on a capacitor, sqrt(kT/C), independent of the resistance that charges it.
Noise power per unit bandwidth, in $\text{V}^2\text{/Hz}$ or $\text{A}^2\text{/Hz}$.
The noise voltage or current, placed at an amplifier's input, that would produce the same output noise from a noiseless amplifier.
The width of an ideal brick-wall filter that passes the same total noise power as the real circuit ($\pi/2$ times the pole frequency for one pole).
The product $A\beta$ around a feedback loop; the closed-loop gain is $\frac{A}{1 + \text{loop gain}}$.
The reduction by (1 + loop gain) in the sensitivity of a closed-loop amplifier's gain to variations in the open-loop gain.
A shunt-shunt feedback amplifier whose output voltage is proportional to the input current; low input and output resistance.
An expression for a feedback circuit's port impedance: $Z = Z_0 \frac{1 + T_{sc}}{1 + T_{oc}}$, with $T_{sc}$ and $T_{oc}$ the loop gains with the port shorted or open.
A high-gain differential amplifier meant to be used with negative feedback.
A single-stage op amp where the input pair and cascode devices are the same polarity, giving the highest gain and lowest noise but the smallest swing.
The maximum rate of change of an amplifier's output, limited by the current available to charge a capacitor ($\mathrm{SR} = I/C$).
Using an auxiliary amplifier to regulate a cascode device and so multiply the output resistance (and gain) without costing voltage headroom.
A loop that senses the average output voltage of a fully differential amplifier and adjusts bias currents to keep it at a set value.
The differential input voltage needed to bring an amplifier's output to zero, caused by device mismatch.
A measure of how well an amplifier ignores variations on the supply voltage.
The amount by which the loop-gain phase is above -180 degrees at the frequency where its magnitude is 1; a measure of stability.
A feedback loop oscillates at a frequency where the loop gain has magnitude one and phase -180 degrees.
Adding capacitors or other elements to an amplifier so that its loop gain falls through 0 dB with enough phase margin.
The effect of Miller compensation in a two-stage amplifier: the first pole moves to lower frequency and the second to higher.
Compensating a two-stage op amp with a capacitor around the second stage, using the Miller effect to create a large dominant-pole capacitance.
A resistor in series with the Miller capacitor that moves the right-half-plane zero to infinity or into the left half plane.
A design approach that uses the ratio of transconductance to drain current as the main sizing variable, valid from weak to strong inversion.
A voltage reference that sums a CTAT base-emitter voltage and a scaled PTAT voltage to cancel temperature dependence, giving about 1.2 V.
Proportional to absolute temperature: a voltage or current that rises linearly with temperature, such as $V_T \ln(n)$.
Complementary to absolute temperature: a voltage that falls with temperature, such as a base-emitter voltage.
The error charge a MOS switch deposits on its load capacitor when it turns off, from its channel charge being expelled.
Output components at integer multiples of the input frequency created by a nonlinear circuit.
Mixing of two or more input tones in a nonlinear circuit to produce sum and difference frequencies.
Random differences between nominally identical devices, falling as 1/sqrt(area) (Pelgrom's law).
An odd number of inverters connected in a loop, oscillating with period $2 N T_d$.
An oscillator whose frequency is set by a control voltage: $\omega_{out} = \omega_0 + K_{VCO} V_{cont}$.
Short-term random fluctuation of an oscillator's phase, seen as spectral skirts around the carrier.
A feedback system that makes an oscillator's phase track a reference, used for clock generation and frequency synthesis.
A circuit that sources or sinks a current into a capacitor in proportion to the phase error; the output stage of a PLL phase detector.
A feedback loop that aligns a clock with a delayed copy by adjusting a delay line rather than an oscillator.
A simulation condition representing the extremes of process variation (for example fast-fast or slow-slow) that a circuit must tolerate.
The limit on carrier speed at high electric field that makes short-channel drain current rise linearly, not quadratically, with overdrive.
A short-channel effect in which the drain voltage lowers the source-channel barrier, reducing $V_{TH}$ and output resistance.
A failure in which a parasitic thyristor in a CMOS structure turns on and shorts the supply to ground.
The patterning step that transfers a mask pattern into light-sensitive resist on a wafer.
Doping a semiconductor by shooting accelerated dopant ions into it.
A layout technique that arranges matched devices symmetrically about a common centre so linear process gradients cancel.
A grounded or biased ring around a circuit that collects substrate currents and isolates it from noise or latch-up.
A MOSFET whose channel carries electrons: it turns on when the gate is raised above the source by more than the threshold voltage.

A MOSFET whose channel carries holes: it turns on when the gate is pulled below the source by more than the magnitude of its threshold voltage. Holes are slower than electrons, so it needs roughly twice the W/L of an NMOS for the same current (hole mobility is about half to a third of electron mobility).
The voltage across the base-emitter junction of a bipolar transistor. At fixed current it falls by about 2 mV per kelvin, which makes it a CTAT quantity used in bandgap references.

A PLL block that compares the reference and feedback clocks and outputs pulses whose width is the phase error. Unlike a plain phase detector it also tells which clock is faster, so the loop can lock from any starting frequency.
A circuit whose output is proportional to the phase difference between two signals; it is the comparison element of a PLL.
The low-pass filter (often a resistor and capacitors) between the charge pump and the VCO. It averages the pulses into a control voltage and sets the loop's dynamics and bandwidth.
A circuit that outputs a clock whose frequency is the input frequency divided by an integer N. In a PLL it lets the output run at N times the reference frequency.
A filter that passes low frequencies and attenuates frequencies above its cutoff, such as an RC network.
A fabrication step that etches shallow trenches around each transistor and fills them with oxide to isolate neighbouring devices. It is the modern replacement for LOCOS.
An older isolation technique that grows thick oxide between active areas. Its bulging edge, the bird's beak, wastes area, which is why shallow trench isolation replaced it.
A family of industry-standard compact MOSFET models used in SPICE simulation. It includes short-channel effects, so it is far more accurate than the square-law equations.
A four-layer p-n-p-n structure that, once triggered, latches on and conducts a large current. It is the parasitic path behind latch-up in CMOS and is also used deliberately in ESD protection.
The input (IIP3) or output (OIP3) level at which the extrapolated third-order intermodulation product would equal the fundamental. A higher value means a more linear circuit.
A process that puts bipolar and CMOS transistors on one chip, combining the high gain and low noise of bipolars with CMOS density.
A bipolar transistor with an n-type emitter and collector and a p-type base. It conducts when the base is about 0.7 V above the emitter.
A bipolar transistor with a p-type emitter and collector and an n-type base. Standard CMOS processes offer a parasitic vertical PNP, which bandgap circuits use.
A three-terminal device, with emitter, base and collector, whose collector current is set exponentially by the base-emitter voltage.
The operating region where $V_{GS}$ is below the threshold voltage and the channel is off, apart from a small subthreshold leakage current.
A linear equivalent circuit that describes how small changes around a bias point behave. For a MOSFET it consists of the current source $g_m v_{gs}$, the resistance $r_o$ and the capacitances.
The current source that joins the sources of a differential pair and sets the total current the pair shares.
The part of a pair of signals that is the same on both: the average of the two. A differential amplifier ideally ignores it.
The difference between the two signals of a pair, which a differential amplifier amplifies.
How much the loop gain could rise at the frequency where the phase reaches -180 degrees before the loop starts to oscillate. It is measured in dB.
The frequency at which the gain magnitude falls to 1 (0 dB). The phase margin is measured here.

A frequency at which a transfer function's numerator is zero so the gain rises toward it by 20 dB per decade. Zeros often come from a signal path that bypasses the amplifier, such as a feedforward capacitor.
A zero that adds phase lag instead of lead while raising the gain. It appears in Miller-compensated stages and can be cancelled with a series resistor.
The fraction of the output fed back to the input in a feedback loop, usually written $\beta$. The loop gain is $A\beta$.
The gain of an amplifier with feedback applied: $A_f = \frac{A}{1 + A\beta}$. For a large loop gain it approaches $1/\beta$.
The gain of an amplifier with no feedback applied.
Noise from the random arrival of charge carriers crossing a barrier such as a pn junction, with mean square current $2qI\,df$.
A measure of the noise a circuit adds, in dB: the ratio of the input signal-to-noise ratio to the output signal-to-noise ratio. A noiseless circuit has 0 dB.
The frequency where two behaviours meet. For noise, it is where flicker noise falls to the level of thermal noise; for a filter, where the gain is 3 dB down.
The ratio of the power in all harmonics of a tone to the power in the fundamental, a measure of nonlinearity.
The input level at which an amplifier's gain has dropped by 1 dB from its small-signal value because of nonlinearity.
The ratio of the largest signal a circuit can handle with acceptable distortion to the smallest signal it can resolve above its noise.
The ratio of the signal level to the strongest unwanted spur or distortion product. It is a common figure for converters and amplifiers.
An oscillator built around an inductor-capacitor resonator. It has lower phase noise than a ring oscillator but needs an inductor and more area.
A capacitor whose value changes with the voltage across it, often a reverse-biased pn junction or MOS device. It tunes the frequency of a VCO.
A parallel inductor and capacitor that resonates at $\frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{LC}}$. Its losses are modelled by a parallel resistance $R_p$.
A measure of how little energy a resonator loses per cycle: the ratio of stored energy to energy lost per cycle, times $2\pi$. A higher $Q$ means a sharper resonance and lower phase noise.
The random variation of a clock's edges from their ideal times. It is the time-domain view of phase noise.
The range of input frequencies over which a PLL can stay locked, or in which it locks quickly without cycle slipping.
The range of input frequencies from which an unlocked PLL can acquire lock.
The frequency range over which a PLL tracks its input. A wider loop follows the reference more closely, while a narrower one filters the reference noise more.
A transistor that connects a signal to a capacitor while the clock is high and isolates it when the clock is low. Its on-resistance and the capacitor set the sampling bandwidth.
An NMOS and a PMOS in parallel, driven by opposite clocks. It keeps the on-resistance low over the whole signal range.
A circuit that uses switches and capacitors, instead of resistors, to process signals in discrete time; the effective resistance of a capacitor switched at $f_{clk}$ is $\frac{1}{f_{clk} C}$.
A circuit that follows an input (track mode) and then freezes its value on a capacitor (hold mode), giving a converter a steady value to measure.
The error when a signal is sampled at less than twice its highest frequency: higher frequencies fold back and appear as lower ones.
The operating regime where $V_{GS}$ is well above threshold, the channel is fully formed and the current follows the square law.
The transition regime between weak and strong inversion, where neither the exponential nor the square-law model is accurate.
A normalized measure of how strongly a transistor is inverted, used to choose a bias point between weak and strong inversion.
Damage caused by carriers accelerated by a high electric field near the drain; they enter the oxide and shift the threshold voltage over time.
A layout technique that splits two matched transistors into interleaved fingers so that gradients across the chip affect both equally.
An unused device placed at the edge of a matched group so the active ones see the same surroundings and etch behaviour.
Damage to a thin gate oxide caused by charge collected on a long metal line that is connected to it during fabrication.
The thin insulating layer between the gate and the channel. Its thickness sets the gate capacitance $C_{ox}$.
Polycrystalline silicon, used for the gate electrode and for resistors.
A lightly n-doped region in a p-type substrate that holds PMOS transistors.
A lightly p-doped region in an n-type substrate that holds NMOS transistors.
The silicon wafer in which the transistors are built. The substrate terminal of a MOSFET is also called the body or bulk.
A region around a pn junction or under a MOS gate that has been emptied of free carriers, leaving fixed charge.
The boundary between p-type and n-type semiconductor, which conducts in one direction.
A two-terminal device that conducts current in one direction. Its current rises exponentially with forward voltage.
One terminal of a bipolar transistor. It supplies the carriers and carries the sum of base and collector current.
The terminal of a bipolar transistor that collects the carriers. Its current is set by the base-emitter voltage.
The increase of bipolar collector current with collector-emitter voltage because the base narrows. It plays the role channel-length modulation plays in a MOSFET.
A logarithmic unit for ratios. For voltage or current gain, $\mathrm{dB} = 20\log_{10}(\text{ratio})$; for power, $10\log_{10}(\text{ratio})$.
A graph of a transfer function's magnitude in dB and its phase against frequency on a logarithmic axis.
The ratio of a circuit's output to its input as a function of frequency; its poles and zeros determine the frequency response.
The impedance seen looking into an amplifier's input, which determines how much it loads the source.
The impedance seen looking into an amplifier's output, which determines how much the load reduces the gain.
The ratio of output voltage to input voltage of an amplifier.
The ratio of output current to input current of an amplifier.
The range of frequencies over which a circuit's gain stays within 3 dB of its low-frequency value.
The time an output takes to get within a specified error band of its final value after a step.
The capacitance an amplifier drives at its output. It sets the output pole and the amplifier's bandwidth and speed.
The DC current that sets the operating point of a transistor and with it $g_m$, $r_o$ and the swing.
The supply voltage left over after the minimum voltages the transistors in a stack need to stay in saturation; it limits the output swing.
The range over which the output can move while every transistor stays in its intended region.
The range of input common-mode voltages over which an amplifier works properly, with the input pair and the tail source in saturation.
A circuit that supplies a nearly constant current regardless of the voltage across it. A transistor in saturation approximates one.
A voltage regulator that keeps its output constant even when the input is only slightly above it, built from a pass transistor and a feedback amplifier.
An amplifier whose input or output can swing nearly the full range between the supplies.
An output stage in which both transistors conduct a little around zero signal and one takes over at larger swings. It drives heavy loads with low standby current.
An extra amplifier that senses a cascode device's source and adjusts its gate to raise the output resistance further, at the cost of power.
The bandwidth of an ideal brick-wall filter that would pass the same noise power as a real filter of unity peak gain. For a first-order low-pass filter it is $\pi/2$ times the -3 dB frequency.
Sampling a signal much faster than the Nyquist rate so quantization noise is spread over a wider band and can be filtered out.
A converter's resolution as measured from its real signal-to-noise-and-distortion ratio, usually lower than its nominal bit count.
The deviation of each step of a converter from the ideal 1 LSB step.
The maximum deviation of a converter's transfer curve from a straight line.
A circuit that multiplies two signals, so frequencies add and subtract. It moves a signal from one frequency to another, as in the Gilbert cell.
The first amplifier in a receiver, designed to add as little noise as possible so the weak input signal is not buried.
Frequencies from a few kilohertz up to hundreds of gigahertz used for wireless communication.
A circuit chain that picks up a weak radio signal and converts it to a usable one; its first blocks are usually an LNA and a mixer.
A physical constant, $1.38 \times 10^{-23}\text{ J/K}$, that links temperature to energy. It appears in thermal noise: $4kTR$.
How easily carriers move under an electric field. A higher mobility gives a higher current for a given W/L; electrons are about 2 to 4 times as mobile as holes.
The gate capacitance per unit area, equal to the oxide permittivity divided by the oxide thickness.
The ratio of a transistor's channel width to its length. The current at a given bias is proportional to it.
A wide transistor split into several narrow gate fingers connected in parallel, which reduces gate resistance and junction capacitance.
Unwanted capacitance between wires and devices that the designer didn't draw but the layout creates.
The capacitance of a reverse-biased pn junction, such as the drain-to-body junction of a MOSFET, which falls as the reverse bias rises.
The capacitance between the gate and the source or drain regions that extend slightly under it.
The capacitance between gate and source, about $\frac{2}{3} W L C_{ox}$ in saturation plus overlap.
The capacitance between gate and drain. It bridges input and output in a common-source stage and is multiplied by the Miller effect.
A sudden transfer of charge between objects at different voltages, which can destroy thin gate oxides. Pads include protection structures to divert it.
Variations in process, supply voltage and temperature, which a design must tolerate.
How much a quantity changes per degree of temperature, for example in ppm per degree.
A simulation repeated many times with random device variations, to see the statistical spread of a circuit's performance.
The standard circuit simulator, which solves a netlist of devices for its DC, AC and transient behaviour.
A node held at a fixed voltage by feedback without being connected to a fixed supply, such as the inverting input of an op amp with feedback.
An op-amp circuit with the input applied through a resistor to the inverting input. The gain is $-\frac{R_2}{R_1}$.
An op-amp circuit with the signal applied to the non-inverting input. The gain is $1 + \frac{R_2}{R_1}$.
A circuit that outputs a logic high or low depending on whether one input is larger than the other. It is a high-gain amplifier or a regenerative latch.
A comparator with hysteresis: it switches at a higher threshold on the way up than on the way down, which stops noise from causing false transitions.
Positive feedback that amplifies a small difference quickly until it reaches full logic levels, as in a latch.
The time between a change at a gate's input and the resulting change at its output. It sets the frequency of a ring oscillator.
The number of gate inputs a single output drives. FO4 delay (an inverter driving four copies of itself) is a technology-independent speed measure.
A circuit that has been reduced to a voltage source in series with a resistance (or, as the Norton form, a current source in parallel).
Two rules for circuits: currents entering a node sum to zero (KCL), and voltages around a loop sum to zero (KVL).

A circuit whose gain rises with frequency roughly as the inverse of a channel's loss, so that a cable or board trace followed by the equalizer has a flat response and the received bits are no longer smeared together.
Gordon Moore's observation that the number of transistors per chip doubles roughly every one and a half to two years, driven by shrinking device dimensions.
The views a designer switches between: device (fields and charge in one transistor), circuit (interacting transistors), architecture (connected building blocks) and system (the whole product).

A single-transistor LC oscillator in which a capacitive divider (C1 from drain to source, C2 from source to ground) feeds the drain swing back to the source; it needs $g_m R_P \ge 4$ at best, against 1 for a cross-coupled pair.
An incremental resistance below zero: raising the voltage across the port lowers its current. Placed across a lossy tank it cancels the loss; a cross-coupled pair presents $-2/g_m$.
An oscillator viewed as a tank in parallel with an active circuit that presents a negative resistance large enough to cancel the tank loss.
The source-grounded member of the family of single-transistor LC oscillators with two capacitors and an inductor; widely used with crystals.
Two transistors whose drains drive each other's gates. It gives positive feedback and a differential resistance of $-2/g_m$, used for LC oscillators, latches and negative-resistance loads.
An LC oscillator in which a cross-coupled pair cancels the tank loss; it starts when $g_m R_P \ge 1$.
An amplifier with an LC tank as its load: the gain $-g_m R_P$ peaks at resonance and is small elsewhere, and the output swings around the supply.
An inductor made of a metal spiral on the chip, typically 100 to 200 µm across, with a Q of roughly 5 to 10 limited by metal resistance.
The span of frequencies a VCO can reach over the allowed control-voltage range; it must cover the application plus process and temperature drift.
The slope $K_{VCO} = \partial\omega_{out}/\partial V_{cont}$ of a VCO's tuning curve, in rad/s/V. A larger gain covers more range but turns control-line noise into more frequency noise.
Biasing a circuit with a copy (replica) placed in a feedback loop, e.g. an op amp sets a triode load so that the replica's swing equals a reference, and the same bias goes to every stage.
A ring-oscillator stage that sums a fast and a slow path and shifts weight between them with the control voltage, giving about a 2:1 delay range at constant swing.
Using a differential pair to drive two current mirrors so their outputs always sum to a constant; it steers current like a stacked pair without its headroom cost.
An NMOS built inside an n-well with source, drain and well tied together; its gate capacitance varies monotonically with voltage and it never forward-biases.
The part of a signal's phase beyond the steady $\omega_0 t$ ramp; for a VCO it is $K_{VCO}\int V_{cont}dt$, so the VCO acts as an integrator $K_{VCO}/s$.
Binary frequency modulation: the carrier frequency toggles between two values according to the data.
A spectral component beside a carrier, e.g. at $\omega_0 \pm \omega_m$ when a VCO's control voltage carries a ripple at $\omega_m$.
The electrical length of a MOSFET's channel, shorter than the drawn gate length because the source and drain diffuse sideways under the gate: $L_{eff} = L_{drawn} - 2L_D$.
An n-type region buried under a p-well so that the NMOS devices inside get their own isolated bulk, at the cost of large spacing rules.
Triode operation with $V_{DS} \ll 2(V_{GS} - V_{TH})$, where the drain current is linear in $V_{DS}$ and the channel acts as a resistor set by the gate voltage.
The resistance of a MOSFET in deep triode: $R_{on} = 1/[\mu C_{ox}(W/L)(V_{GS} - V_{TH})]$.
The point where the channel charge at the drain end falls to zero because the gate-to-channel voltage there drops below the threshold; beyond it the drain current saturates.
The long-channel saturation equation $I_D = \frac{1}{2}\mu_n C_{ox}(W/L)(V_{GS} - V_{TH})^2$.
The minimum drain-source voltage that keeps a MOSFET saturated, $V_{D,sat} = V_{GS} - V_{TH}$; it is headroom the circuit must leave across the device.
The constant $\gamma = \sqrt{2q\epsilon_{si}N_{sub}}/C_{ox}$ that sets how much the threshold rises with source-bulk voltage, typically 0.3 to 0.4 $\text{V}^{1/2}$.
Breakdown in a short-channel MOSFET where the drain depletion region reaches the source's and a large uncontrolled current flows.
The part of a source/drain junction capacitance due to the junction's perimeter, specified per unit length and added to the bottom-plate (area) part.
The small-signal gain from bulk-source voltage to drain current, $g_{mb} = \eta g_m$ with $\eta = \gamma/(2\sqrt{2\Phi_F + V_{SB}})$, typically around 0.25.
The simplest SPICE MOSFET model, based on the square law with body effect and channel-length modulation, defined by parameters such as VTO, GAMMA, PHI, LAMBDA, TOX and the junction capacitances.
A three-dimensional MOSFET whose channel is a thin vertical silicon fin with the gate wrapped over three sides; its width comes in steps of one fin, $W_F + 2H_F$.
The state of an MOS structure with the gate driven so that majority carriers pile up at the surface; its capacitance per area is then $C_{ox}$.
A signal measured between one node and a fixed potential, usually ground.
The average (bias) voltage of the two nodes of a differential signal, about which they swing in opposite directions.
Two matched transistors whose sources share a tail current source; it amplifies the difference between its two inputs and largely ignores their common level.
A differential pair with resistance in its sources, which widens the linear input range by about the tail current times the resistance while lowering the gain.
The appearance of a differential output error caused by a common-mode input change, because the two halves of a differential circuit are mismatched.
An amplifier whose gain is set by a control voltage or current, for example a differential pair whose tail current is varied.
A circuit whose output is proportional to the product of two inputs of either polarity; the Gilbert cell is the standard CMOS example.
The slope $K_{PD}$ of a phase detector's average output against phase difference, in V/rad; $V_0/\pi$ for an XOR gate with swing $V_0$.
A flip-flop used as a phase detector: its average output jumps between two values as the phase error changes sign, giving very high gain at zero and none elsewhere.

The constant phase difference a locked PLL keeps between input and output: $(\omega_{in}-\omega_0)/(K_{PD}K_{VCO})$ in a type I loop; ideally zero in a charge-pump loop but set by up/down mismatch in practice.
A PLL whose loop gain has one pole at the origin (from the VCO); it has a finite static phase error and its settling rate $\zeta\omega_n = \omega_{LPF}/2$ is set by the filter.
The parameter $\zeta$ of a second-order system $s^2 + 2\zeta\omega_n s + \omega_n^2$; below about 0.5 the step response rings strongly, PLLs typically use 0.7 to 1.
The parameter $\omega_n$ of a second-order system $s^2 + 2\zeta\omega_n s + \omega_n^2$; for a charge-pump PLL $\omega_n = \sqrt{I_PK_{VCO}/(2\pi C_PM)}$.
A PLL whose loop gain has two poles at the origin (charge pump into a capacitor, plus the VCO); it has zero static phase error and needs a series resistor in the filter to be stable.

Adding a frequency-detection path to a PLL so the VCO is first pulled near the input frequency, after which the phase loop locks; it widens the acquisition (capture) range from about $\omega_{LPF}$ to the VCO tuning range.
A range of small phase errors to which a phase detector and charge pump give no output, so the loop does not correct them and the VCO phase wanders (jitter). PFD reset pulses remove it.
Redistribution of charge when a switch connects capacitors at different voltages; in a charge pump it makes the control voltage jump when the switches close.
Driving a node with a buffered copy of another node's voltage so the two stay equal, e.g. holding a charge pump's internal nodes at the control voltage while its switches are off.
How a PLL passes phase wander to its output: low-pass from the input, high-pass from the VCO, with the loop bandwidth as the dividing line.
A chain of delay stages whose delay is set by a control voltage; the controlled element of a delay-locked loop.
A PLL with a programmable feedback divider: $f_{out} = Mf_{REF}$ with the accuracy of the reference, stepping in increments of $f_{REF}$.
Extracting a clock from a data stream with a narrow-band PLL so the data can be retimed when no separate clock is sent.
The time offset between a clock and the signal or clock it should align with, e.g. the delay added by a large on-chip clock buffer; a PLL or DLL with the buffer inside the loop removes it.
One accurately generated current from which a circuit's bias currents are copied by current mirrors.
A standard-size transistor repeated in parallel or series to set current ratios in mirrors, more accurately than drawing devices of different widths.

A current mirror with a cascode device on the output so its drain voltage matches the reference device's; accurate and high in output resistance but needing about two overdrives plus a threshold of headroom.
A cascode current mirror whose reference branch is itself a cascode, letting the output work down to about two overdrive voltages.
A differential pair loaded by a current mirror, giving a single-ended output with gain about gm(ro2 ∥ ro4).
Passing a signal between stages through a series capacitor so each stage can set its own DC bias; it forms a high-pass filter with the bias resistance.

The rule that a linear stage's voltage gain is $A_v = -G_m R_{out}$, where $G_m$ is the output current per input volt with the output shorted to AC ground and $R_{out}$ is the output resistance with the input zeroed.
A transistor in saturation used as the load of a gain stage; it presents a high small-signal resistance $r_o$ with only a small DC drop, giving a CS gain of $-g_{m1}(r_{o1} \parallel r_{o2})$.
A transistor with gate tied to drain used as a load; it looks like about $1/g_m$, so the CS gain is a ratio of device sizes and nearly bias-independent.

A CMOS inverter biased in its high-gain region, with both transistors driven by the input; its gain is $-(g_{m1}+g_{m2})(r_{o1} \parallel r_{o2})$, but its bias current is set by the supply and it amplifies supply noise.
A transistor held in deep triode and used as a load resistor; it saves headroom but its value depends on process, temperature and an accurate gate bias.
A change in the DC level of a signal; a source follower shifts its input down by $V_{GS}$, which costs headroom but can bring a signal near a rail into another stage's input range.
The cascode device's attenuation of output voltage changes before they reach the input device's drain, by about $(g_m + g_{mb})r_o$; it is lost if the cascode device enters triode.

Two stacked transistors sharing one gate voltage. It acts as a true cascode only if the top device's threshold is lower than the bottom one's by more than the top device's overdrive; otherwise it behaves like one longer transistor.
Three stacked devices that raise the output resistance further, at the cost of a minimum output voltage of three overdrives.
Shrinking all dimensions and voltages by $\alpha$ and raising doping by $\alpha$, so fields stay constant: current and capacitance fall by $\alpha$, delay by $\alpha$, density rises by $\alpha^2$.
Shrinking device dimensions while keeping the supply and threshold voltages fixed; fields grow by the scaling factor, worsening breakdown and short-channel effects.
The gate-voltage change per decade of subthreshold drain current, $S = 2.3V_T(1 + C_d/C_{ox})$; at least about 60 mV/dec at room temperature.
The drop of threshold voltage at short channel lengths, because the source and drain depletion regions terminate part of the channel depletion charge.
A rise of threshold voltage as channel length shrinks from long values, caused by halo implants that dope the channel ends more heavily.
A heavily doped region implanted around the source and drain junctions to limit drain depletion into the channel.
The fall of carrier mobility at high gate field, modelled as $\mu_{eff} = \mu_0/[1 + \theta(V_{GS}-V_{TH})]$; it lowers current and $g_m$ and adds odd-order distortion.
Generation of electron-hole pairs by energetic (hot) carriers colliding with the lattice near the drain; it adds a drain-to-substrate current and lowers the output resistance at high drain voltage.
A MOS model that references all voltages to the bulk, treats source and drain symmetrically, and uses one current equation from weak to strong inversion.
The simple gate-capacitance model with fixed partitions (2/3, 1/2); it does not conserve charge in transient simulation.
How a MOS model splits the channel charge between source and drain (for example 40/60, 50/50 or 0/100 in BSIM).

A floating impedance Z between nodes with gain $A_v = V_Y/V_X$ can be replaced by $Z/(1 - A_v)$ at X and $Z/(1 - 1/A_v)$ at Y. Using the low-frequency gain is the Miller approximation; it can drop zeros and add false poles.
The pole at the diode-connected node of a current-mirror load, at about $g_{m3}/C_E$. In a differential pair with an active load it comes with a left-half-plane zero at twice its frequency.
A capacitor's resistance-times-capacitance product found with the input zeroed and every other capacitor removed. Their sum approximates the inverse of the dominant pole, or of the -3 dB bandwidth.

Middlebrook's result for adding one impedance $Z_1$ to a circuit with known transfer function H: $G = H\,(1 + Z_{out,0}/Z_1)/(1 + Z_{in,0}/Z_1)$, where $Z_{in,0}$ is found with the input zeroed and $Z_{out,0}$ with the output nulled.

A source follower driven from a large gate resistance, whose output impedance rises with frequency like an inductor of about $(C_{GS}/g_m)(R_S - 1/g_m)$. Used to extend bandwidth; it is lossy and costs headroom.
When one pole is far below the others, the inverse of the s coefficient of the denominator gives that pole, and the ratio of the s and s-squared coefficients gives the next one.
Resistivity divided by layer thickness, $R_{□} = \rho/t$, in ohms per square; a line has $R = R_{□}L/W$.
Growing a single-crystal silicon ingot by slowly drawing a rotating seed out of doped molten silicon; the ingot is sliced into wafers.
A light-sensitive film used in lithography; after exposure through a mask and development, it covers some regions and opens others.
An implant under the field oxide that raises the threshold of the parasitic thick-oxide transistor between neighbouring devices.
Heating the wafer after implantation to repair lattice damage; it also diffuses dopants, causing lateral diffusion under the gate.
Deep penetration of implanted ions travelling along a crystal axis; avoided by tilting the beam or wafer by about 7 degrees.
A well whose doping peaks below the surface (from a high-energy implant): low resistance at the bottom against latch-up, light doping at the top for low junction capacitance.
Depositing a film (polysilicon, oxide) from a gas that reacts in a furnace; done at low pressure for uniformity.
A precise etching method in which ions produced in a gas bombard the wafer.
Forming source and drain after the gate so the gate itself masks the implant; the junctions start exactly at the gate edges regardless of mask misalignment.
A thin metal-silicon compound over poly and diffusion that cuts their sheet resistance about tenfold; oxide spacers make it self-aligned.
A shallow implant after gate oxidation that moves the native thresholds of NMOS and PMOS to their target values.
Penetration of aluminium from a large contact through a shallow junction into the substrate, shorting the diode; avoided with arrays of small contacts.
The protective glass layer over a finished die, opened only over the bond pads.
A polysilicon resistor made by keeping silicide off part of a poly line: fifty to a few hundred ohms per square, linear and low in parasitic capacitance but about ±20% in absolute value.
A resistor made of n-well, about 1 kΩ per square, with large spread, large substrate capacitance and voltage-dependent value.
A MOSFET with source and drain tied, used as a dense but voltage-dependent capacitor; its channel adds series resistance with time constant about $L^2/[4\mu(V_{GS}-V_{TH})]$.
The capacitance from a capacitor's lower plate to the substrate, a few to 20 percent of the main capacitance depending on the structure.
Gradual transport of metal atoms by high current density, which leaves voids and eventually opens a wire; limits current to roughly 2 mA per µm of width for aluminium.
The part of a wire's capacitance from field lines leaving its edges and sides; comparable to or larger than the parallel-plate part for narrow lines.
The reduction, by the factor $1 + \beta A$, of the closed-loop gain's sensitivity to changes in the open-loop gain $A$.
An amplifier that converts an input voltage to an output current, with gain $G_m = I_{out}/V_{in}$ in siemens. Ideally it has infinite input and output impedance.
Feedback that senses the output voltage and returns a voltage in series with the input; it raises $R_{in}$ and lowers $R_{out}$ by $1 + \beta A$.
Feedback that senses the output current (usually across a small series resistor) and returns a voltage; it raises both $R_{in}$ and $R_{out}$.
Feedback that senses the output voltage and returns a current to the input node; it lowers both $R_{in}$ and $R_{out}$.
Feedback that senses the output current and returns a current to the input node; it lowers $R_{in}$ and raises $R_{out}$.
The change in an amplifier's gain caused by the finite input and output impedances of the feedback network attached to it; the two-port method includes it when the loop is opened.
A linear circuit with an input and an output port, described by Z, Y, H or G parameters; used to model the forward amplifier and feedback network.

For one controlled source $g_m V_1$: with the input zeroed and the source replaced by an independent one, minus $g_m$ times the controlling voltage returned per unit source. It equals the loop gain when one loop passes through that device.
Exact closed-loop analysis that keeps one transistor's source as $I_1$: $V_{out}/V_{in} = A + g_m BC/(1 - g_m D)$, with A and C found at $g_m = 0$ and B and D at zero input.
$H = H_\infty T/(1+T) + H_0/(1+T)$: the ideal gain $H_\infty$ (infinite loop gain) weighted by $T/(1+T)$ plus direct feedthrough $H_0$ suppressed by $1+T$.
A loop-gain and transfer-function method that injects a series voltage and a shunt current inside an unbroken loop, separating forward and reverse loop gains.
Thermal noise of the polysilicon gate, equivalent to a lumped resistor $R_G/3$ in series with the gate; splitting the device into N fingers divides it by $N^2$.

The parallel current source that, with the input-referred noise voltage, represents a noisy two-port; found by leaving the input open. It matters when the source impedance squared approaches $\overline{V_{n,in}^2}/\overline{I_{n,in}^2}$.
The resistance $R_T$ whose thermal noise $4kTR_T$ equals a circuit's input-referred thermal noise; $\gamma/g_m + 1/(g_m^2R_D)$ for a CS stage.
Noise waveforms that share a common origin, so they add as voltages rather than powers. Independent devices give uncorrelated noise, whose powers add.
Doubling transistor widths and currents and halving resistors: gain and swing stay fixed, input-referred noise power halves, and power doubles.
The minimum widths, spacings, enclosures and extensions (and some maximum sizes) that a layout must obey so it can be fabricated reliably despite process tolerances.
The distributed resistance of the poly gate, about one third of its end-to-end value when contacted at one end; it adds thermal noise and is reduced with more fingers or double-sided contacts.
Asymmetry between source and drain caused by the gate blocking part of a tilted implant; matched devices must be shadowed identically.
A common-centroid arrangement with each of two devices split in halves placed on the diagonals of a 2 × 2 grid, cancelling linear gradients in both directions.
Mechanical stress from the oxide-filled isolation trench that alters nearby transistors' characteristics; reduced by dummy fingers at the ends of a device.
Doping nonuniformity near a well edge, caused by implant ions scattering off the masking layer, which changes devices placed close to the edge.
An identical building block repeated to build ratioed devices, so ratios are set by integer counts rather than by drawn dimensions.
Unwanted coupling of a signal from one wire into another through their mutual capacitance (or inductance); reduced by differential signaling and shielding.
A large metal square, typically 70 to 100 µm across and made of the top metal layers, where a bond wire connects to the chip.
An ESD test model of a person: about a hundred picofarads charged to thousands of volts, discharging through about 1.5 kΩ.
Noise injected into the shared substrate by switching circuits that reaches analog transistors, mainly through body effect.
Transient movement of on-chip supply or ground caused by switching currents through package inductance, $\Delta V = L\,dI/dt$.
The thin wire (25 to 50 µm) from a pad to the package, with roughly 1 nH of inductance per millimetre.
A capacitor between supply and ground (or on a bias node) that supplies transient current locally; it can resonate with package inductance unless damped.
A bond from a ground pad down to a ground plane under the die, giving a low-inductance ground connection.
Coupling between two current paths by their shared magnetic flux; it adds noise between bond wires and changes the inductance of parallel wires to $(L_S + M)/2$.
In a folded-cascode amplifier, the node where the input transistor's drain current enters the source of the opposite-type cascode; its capacitance sets the main non-dominant pole.
An op amp with a high-gain first stage followed by a common-source second stage, giving high gain and near rail-to-rail output swing at the cost of speed and the need for compensation.
A cascode whose gate is driven by an auxiliary amplifier sensing its source, multiplying the output resistance by about $A_1 + 1$ without extra headroom.
The average of the two outputs of a differential amplifier; in high-gain stages it is undefined without common-mode feedback.

Extracting the output common-mode level of a differential amplifier, by resistors, source followers plus resistors, capacitors, triode transistors or differential pairs, independently of the differential signal.
Large-signal operation in which an op amp's input pair is fully switched and a capacitor charges with a fixed current, so the output ramps at the slew rate instead of settling exponentially.
Exponential approach to the final value, with a slope proportional to the remaining error; settling to relative error $\epsilon$ takes $\tau\ln(1/\epsilon)$.

A stage whose output current can rise well above its quiescent bias during large transients, for example by driving the load current source with the opposite signal, raising the slew rate for little static power.
NMOS and PMOS differential pairs in parallel so that one works when the other turns off near a rail, extending the input common-mode range to both supplies.
A small circuit that injects current into a self-biased reference at power-up so it cannot remain in its zero-current (degenerate) operating point, and then turns itself off.
A loop of two current mirrors whose reference current is a copy of its own output, with a resistor that fixes the current level, making the current nearly independent of the supply voltage.

A bias scheme in which the transconductance of the biased transistors is set by a resistor ($g_m = \frac{2}{R_S}(1 - 1/\sqrt{K})$) rather than by mobility or threshold, keeping $g_m$ stable over process and temperature.
Techniques that cancel the second-order temperature dependence (bowing) left in a first-order bandgap reference, which comes mainly from the non-linear temperature dependence of $V_{BE}$.
A bandgap reference that adds a PTAT current and a CTAT current and converts the sum to a voltage with a resistor, so its output (and supply) can be well below the 1.2 V of a classic bandgap.

The bipolar transistor available in a standard n-well CMOS process: p+ diffusion as emitter, n-well as base and the grounded p-substrate as collector. It provides the junctions for CMOS bandgap references.
The error step coupled onto a sampling capacitor by the clock edge through a switch's gate overlap capacitance; roughly $V_{CK}WC_{ov}/(WC_{ov} + C_H)$ and independent of the signal.
A half-width transistor with source and drain shorted, clocked opposite to a sampling switch, that absorbs the channel charge the switch injects and cancels its clock feedthrough.

Switching scheme in which the switch at the op-amp (virtual-ground) side of the sampling capacitor opens first, so its signal-independent charge sets the sample and later switches cannot disturb the stored charge; the capacitor's bottom plate is kept on driven nodes.

A switched-capacitor sample-and-hold that samples the input on a capacitor with the op amp in unity feedback and then flips the capacitor around the op amp, giving an output equal to the sampled input with input-independent charge injection.
An integrator in which a capacitor switched between the input and the op amp's virtual ground replaces the input resistor, adding $(C_1/C_2)V_{in}$ to the output each clock period.
A capacitor alternately connected to two nodes at a clock rate $f_{CK}$; it moves an average current $C_Sf_{CK}(V_A - V_B)$ and so behaves like a resistor $1/(C_Sf_{CK})$.

A switched-capacitor stage in which two equal capacitors sample the input and one is then placed in feedback while the other dumps its charge into it, giving a gain of two with a feedback factor near one half.
The frequency at which the loop-gain magnitude $|\beta H|$ falls to one (0 dB); the phase margin is read there.
The frequency at which the loop-gain phase reaches $-180^{\circ}$; a stable loop has its gain below one there.
The paths traced in the s-plane by a feedback system's closed-loop poles as the loop gain is varied.
Lowering an amplifier's dominant pole (for example with load capacitance) until the gain crosses unity near or below the first non-dominant pole, giving adequate phase margin.
A closely spaced pole and zero, typically from imperfect pole-zero cancellation, which leaves a slow, small-amplitude tail in the step response.
Compensation in which the Miller capacitor returns output current through a common-gate transistor to the first-stage node, so no feedforward path exists and the right-half-plane zero disappears.
Connecting the compensation capacitor from the output to the low-impedance source of the first stage's cascode transistor, raising both the zero and the non-dominant pole.
An open-loop-stable feedback system is stable if and only if the polar plot of $\beta H(s)$ around the right half plane does not encircle $-1$.
If a closed contour encloses Z zeros and P poles of F(s) clockwise, the image of the contour under F encircles the origin Z minus P times clockwise.
Stability that holds only for a band of loop gains, so that reducing the gain (not only raising it) can make the loop oscillate; it arises when the phase crosses -180 degrees several times.
The empirical rule that the random mismatch between two identically drawn transistors falls with the square root of their area: $\sigma(\Delta V_{TH}) = A_{VTH}/\sqrt{WL}$.
Techniques that measure an amplifier's offset in a dedicated clock phase, store it on capacitors and subtract it during normal operation; they also suppress low-frequency noise.
Taking two closely spaced samples, the first of the offset or reset level and the second of the signal, and subtracting them, so that offset and noise slower than the sample spacing cancel.
Linearization by following a nonlinear V-to-I stage with an I-to-V stage that has the inverse characteristic, such as a square-law differential pair loaded by diode-connected square-law devices.
The dependence of a capacitor's value on its voltage, which makes stored charge a nonlinear function of voltage and distorts switched-capacitor circuits whose gain is not one.

Sizing method for short-channel devices: simulate one reference transistor's $I_D$, $g_m$ and $r_O$ once, then obtain each circuit device by scaling its width and current by the same factor at the same overdrive.
Drain current per unit width, $I_D/W$. Scaling width and current together keeps it, the overdrive and $g_m/I_D$ constant, so $g_m$ scales linearly with the width.
The fractional difference between a feedback amplifier's actual closed-loop gain and its ideal ratio, about $1/(\beta A_0)$ for open-loop gain $A_0$ and feedback factor $\beta$.

The requirement that the common-mode feedback loop of a fully differential op amp be stable on its own; its loop gain is measured with the differential feedback in place and is often compensated with a capacitor at the error amplifier's output.

The range of phase error near $\pm 2\pi$ in which a PFD misses input edges that arrive during its reset pulse and reads the error with the wrong sign; it limits the PFD's top frequency to about $1/(2t_{rst})$.
The short time both PFD outputs are high before the AND gate clears them; it removes the dead zone but adds charge-pump noise, mismatch charge and blind zone.
A dynamic CMOS flip-flop style clocked by a single phase; small and fast, used for high-speed PFDs and prescalers, but needs a minimum clock frequency.
A phase-frequency detector built from precharged nodes instead of flip-flops (Johansson, 1998); very fast and small, with the reset built into the logic.
A small constant current added at the charge-pump output so a fractional-N loop locks with the PFD always on one side of zero, avoiding its nonlinearity, at the cost of more ripple.
A bang-bang phase detector for clock and data recovery that samples data twice per bit and once at the edge between, reporting early, late or no transition.
A linear phase detector for clock recovery from random data that compares a pulse proportional to phase error with a fixed half-period reference pulse.

A phase detector in which the reference edge samples the VCO waveform directly, so no divider is needed in lock and detector noise is not multiplied by $N^2$; it needs a frequency-locked loop for acquisition.
A circuit that measures a time interval digitally, typically in inverter delays; the phase detector of an all-digital PLL, whose resolution sets its in-band noise floor.
A programmable delay that shifts an edge by a digitally set time; used to cancel the predictable phase error in fractional-N digital and sampling PLLs.
An oscillator tuned by a digital word (switched capacitors or inverters, often with sigma-delta dithering for fine steps) instead of a control voltage.
A PLL with a time-to-digital converter or bang-bang detector, a digital loop filter and a digitally controlled oscillator in place of the PFD, charge pump, RC filter and VCO.

A PLL's in-band phase noise referred to a 1 Hz comparison frequency and $N = 1$, so that the in-band floor is $\mathrm{FoM}_{1Hz} + 10\log_{10}f_{PFD} + 20\log_{10}N$; good chips reach about $-230$ dBc/Hz.

$10\log_{10}[(\sigma_t/1\text{ s})^2 (P/1\text{ mW})]$, a PLL benchmark (Gao et al., 2009) combining rms jitter and power; lower is better: about $-235$ to $-245$ dB for good charge-pump PLLs, $-250$ to $-255$ dB for the best designs.
A charge pump whose current sources stay on and are steered either to the output or to a dummy node held at the output voltage, which avoids charge sharing and speeds switching.
A charge pump with two outputs and common-mode feedback, driving a differential loop filter and VCO control; common-mode injection and leakage cancel and the swing doubles.
A pair of sidebands at $\pm f_{ref}$ around a PLL's output, caused by control-voltage ripple from charge-pump mismatch, switching errors or leakage.
A difference between a charge pump's UP and DN currents, from device mismatch and from output-voltage dependence; it causes static phase offset and reference spurs.

A charge-pump technique (Lee, Keel, Lim and Kim, 2000) in which an error amplifier forces a replica branch's middle node to the output voltage, making the DN current equal the UP current at any output voltage.
A passive loop filter with an extra series resistor and shunt capacitor after the second-order RC network, adding a pole that attenuates reference spurs at some cost in phase margin.
A PLL loop filter built around an op-amp integrator, which holds the charge-pump output at a fixed voltage and lets the VCO control swing rail to rail, at the cost of op-amp noise and power.

A model of oscillator phase noise, $\mathcal{L} = 10\log[\frac{2FkT}{P_s}(1 + (\frac{f_0}{2Q\Delta f})^2)(1 + \frac{\Delta f_{1/f^3}}{\Delta f})]$, showing improvement with tank $Q$ squared and signal power.

The function $\Gamma(\omega_0 t)$ giving how much an injected charge shifts an oscillator's phase depending on when in the cycle it arrives (Hajimiri and Lee, 1998); its rms and DC values set the $1/f^2$ and $1/f^3$ phase noise.
The offset at which an oscillator's phase noise changes from 30 to 20 dB per decade; equal to the devices' $1/f$ corner times $(\Gamma_{dc}/\Gamma_{rms})^2$, so symmetric waveforms lower it.

$-\mathcal{L}(\Delta f) + 20\log_{10}(f_0/\Delta f) - 10\log_{10}(P/1\text{ mW})$, which compares oscillators of different frequency and power; LC VCOs reach about 180 to 196 dBc/Hz, rings 150 to 165.

aliases: period jitter of a free-running oscillator
definition: The rms timing error a free-running oscillator accumulates over one period, $\Delta f\sqrt{\mathcal{L}(\Delta f)}/f_0^{3/2}$ in its $1/f^2$ region.
The operating range of an LC oscillator in which its swing grows in proportion to the tail current, before devices enter triode or the swing reaches the supply.
The operating range of an LC oscillator in which the swing is clipped by the supply or by devices entering triode, so more current no longer improves phase noise.
An LC oscillator with both NMOS and PMOS cross-coupled pairs, which reuses its current for twice the swing of an NMOS-only core in the current-limited regime.

Adding a large capacitor and a $2\omega_0$-resonant inductor at an LC oscillator's tail (Hegazi, Sjöland and Abidi, 2001) so the tail source's noise and the switches' loading no longer degrade phase noise.

An LC oscillator whose cross-coupled devices are biased to conduct only near the voltage peaks, with a large tail capacitor, giving a theoretical 3.9 dB phase-noise improvement at the same current (Mazzanti and Andreani, 2008).
A tail-less LC oscillator whose large switches pull each side hard to ground for half a cycle, working from very low supplies with low phase noise but high supply pushing (Fanori and Andreani, 2013).
An LC oscillator with an extra tank resonance at the third harmonic that squares up the waveform and lowers its effective impulse sensitivity (Babaie and Staszewski, 2013).
A ring-oscillator delay stage with series current-limiting transistors whose control current sets the stage delay and so the frequency.
A differential delay-cell load of a diode-connected PMOS in parallel with an equal biased PMOS (Maneatis, 1996), giving a delay set by the control voltage with good supply rejection.
A PLL (Maneatis, 1996) whose charge-pump current and loop-filter resistance are derived from the VCO's own bias, so damping is fixed and bandwidth is a constant fraction of the operating frequency.

Forcing an oscillator's phase to follow a periodic injected signal near its own frequency or a sub-harmonic; with a reference injected into a ring every cycle, jitter accumulation is reset each period.
A ring oscillator in which one edge per reference cycle is replaced by the clean reference edge, combining a ring's area with much lower jitter.
Digitally switched capacitors across an LC tank that choose one of many overlapping frequency bands, leaving fine tuning to a small varactor.
A routine run before a PLL closes that counts VCO cycles over a reference window and searches the capacitor-bank code that puts the VCO near its target frequency.
The change of an oscillator's frequency with its supply voltage, in Hz/V, which turns supply noise into frequency noise.
The shift of an oscillator's frequency caused by its load or by a strong nearby signal coupling into it, such as a transmitter's power amplifier.
Conversion of amplitude variations into phase variations, for example by a varactor whose capacitance depends on the swing; it turns amplitude noise into phase noise.
Splitting a VCO's varactor into units biased at staggered DC voltages so the combined tuning curve, and so $K_{VCO}$, is flatter.
